finding: Worst station-year missingness
reading: Tap Mun and 2023 carry the missingness; every other station-year is near 1%.

finding: Station-years relying most on substituted values
value: Tuen Mun 2026 17.7%; North 2026 6.4%; Central 2026 6.2%; North 2022 5.5%; Sham Shui Po 2022 5.3%
reading: Substitution is not uniform: a few station-years are mostly borrowed data, so a station ranking must be read with that in mind.

finding: AQHI is dominated by the low band
reading: The index is discrete 1-10; any mean near 3 is a low-air-pollution baseline, and 7+ is the health-relevant tail.

finding: Longest continuous outage
reading: The export has three outage shapes: 38 absent dates, 17 all-station blank days in 2023, and a Tap Mun outage in Sep-Oct 2023.

finding: Substitution is not neutral for the level
reading: Borrowed values sit slightly away from own measurements, so station means mix two data-generating processes; report a sensitivity without them.

finding: Annual territory mean is flat, not trending
reading: Year-to-year spread is small relative to the seasonal swing visible in the same panel.

finding: Seasonal cycle is the largest signal
reading: Summer is the clean season in this index; the annual mean hides a swing about twice the between-year spread.

finding: Weekday/weekend difference is negligible
reading: Day-of-week is not a useful lever for the scenario; hour and season are.

finding: Persistence decays slowly at hourly scale
value: hourly lag1 0.986, lag24 0.748; daily lag1 0.819, lag7 0.332
reading: Today is a good predictor of the next few hours; a week ahead is nearly independent at the daily level.

finding: A construction change sits inside the series
reading: EPD updated the ozone risk factor on 2025-03-22. Any 2025-2026 level must be compared with that caveat, not read as an air-quality trend.

finding: No defensible monotonic trend in five annual means
reading: With five points and a mid-series method change, the trend estimate is not separable from year-to-year weather variability.

finding: High days cluster in spring and autumn, not winter alone
value: Winter 27.2%, Spring 31.4%, Summer 11.7%, Autumn 29.7% of 401 high days
reading: Summer is clearly the clean season, but the worst months include April and September, so 'winter is bad' is the wrong rule.

finding: One spring 2023 episode dominates the record
value: 2023-02-26 to 2023-03-18, 21 days, peak 10; 2023 had 115 high days vs 56-70 in the other full years
reading: The 2023 spring episode is the single largest pattern in the record; a five-year average hides it.

finding: Most episodes are short
reading: A one-day-ahead warning covers most episodes; multi-day episodes are rare but carry the highest peaks.

finding: A high day nearly triples tomorrow's odds
reading: Persistence is real but not decisive; the day after a high day is the only day with materially elevated risk.

finding: Even the hourly episodes are short
reading: A bad air day is a burst of hours, not a constant condition; timing the outdoor window matters.

finding: Roadside stations sit above general stations
reading: The 18-station average mixes two exposure regimes; the scenario should name the station or district, not 'Hong Kong'.

finding: Stations are not one homogeneous network
reading: Co-movement is high but not uniform; a territory mean smooths real district differences.

finding: Spatial spread widens on dirty days
value: daily range median 0.96, max 3.7; corr(range, territory mean) 0.46
reading: A territory mean hides that one district can be several bands worse than another on the same day.

finding: The roadside gap is largest in the evening
reading: A general-station reading understates roadside exposure exactly when people commute.

finding: The heaviest afternoon tail is not the highest-mean station
value: Tuen Mun 2.95% of hours >=7, Tap Mun 2.86%, Causeway Bay 1.35%; amplitude-tail r = 0.83
reading: Rural and western New Territories stations swing harder in the afternoon and cross the high band more often, while roadside stations have a higher average but a thinner tail.

finding: The safest daytime cells are early morning, and the spread across cells is large
reading: Timing and month matter more than the annual average; the worst cell is more than 20 times the best.

finding: Month-level risk is driven by a few years, not a stable monthly law
value: April: 0.0% in 2024 vs 9.2% in 2025; September: 0.1% in 2025 vs 14.9% in 2022
reading: April 2025 and September 2022 create the month-level tail; do not promise a quiet September on the strength of the pooled average.

finding: Summer has the fewest high days, spring and autumn the most
reading: June and August are the safest months; January, April and September carry the highest share of high days.

finding: The best daytime six-hour window is early morning in every month
reading: 06:00-11:59 is the lowest-risk block; the afternoon build-up is the thing to avoid.
